Uniform Circular Motion: In uniform circular motion an object moves around a circle at constant speed. Although the speed is constant, the direction of the velocity keeps changing, so the velocity changes and the object accelerates. The velocity is always tangent to the circle. The period T is the time for one revolution and the frequency f = 1 / T is the number of revolutions per second, measured in hertz. The speed is the circumference divided by the period: v = 2 pi r / T = 2 pi r f. The angular speed omega = 2 pi / T, in radians per second, and v = omega r.
Centripetal Force and Acceleration: An object in uniform circular motion accelerates toward the center of the circle. This centripetal acceleration is a_c = v^2 / r = 4 pi^2 r / T^2. By Newton's second law a net force toward the center, the centripetal force, is needed: F_c = m v^2 / r. It is not a new kind of force; it is provided by tension, gravity, friction or the normal force. For a car on a flat curve friction provides the force, so the maximum speed is v = sqrt(mu g r). If the force stops, the object moves off in a straight line tangent to the circle. 'Centrifugal force' is only the feeling of inertia in a rotating frame.
Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation: Every mass attracts every other mass with a force that is proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers: F = G m1 m2 / r^2, where G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2. The forces on the two masses are equal and opposite (Newton's third law) and always attractive. Doubling one mass doubles the force; doubling the distance divides the force by 4. Because G is so small, gravity between everyday objects is tiny and only noticeable when one mass is huge, such as a planet. The same law explains why objects fall and why the Moon orbits Earth.
Gravitational Fields and Weight: A mass creates a gravitational field around it. The field strength g at a distance r from a mass M is g = G M / r^2, in newtons per kilogram, which equals the free-fall acceleration in m/s^2. At Earth's surface g = 9.8 N/kg; it decreases with altitude and is about 1.6 N/kg on the Moon. Weight is the gravitational force on an object, W = m g; mass does not change with location but weight does. Astronauts in orbit feel weightless not because gravity is absent but because they are in free fall together with their spacecraft. On Earth's surface the combination G M / R^2 gives 9.8 m/s^2 with M = 5.97 x 10^24 kg and R = 6.37 x 10^6 m.
Orbits and Kepler's Laws: A satellite orbits because it is falling around Earth: it moves sideways fast enough that the surface curves away beneath it. Gravity provides the centripetal force, so G M m / r^2 = m v^2 / r and the orbital speed is v = sqrt(G M / r); higher orbits are slower and have longer periods. Kepler's laws describe planetary motion. First, orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus. Second, a line from the planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves fastest when closest. Third, T^2 is proportional to r^3, so T^2 / r^3 is the same for all planets around the same star. A geostationary satellite has a period of 24 h and stays above one point on the equator.
